extracted.intended_audience: academic psychologists, researchers studying peer review and confirmation bias, and readers of Current Psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging short research abstracts in psychology — focusing on how topic, methodological quality, and reported results (confirmation/disconfirmation) influence perceived quality and appropriateness. Based on an experimental study manipulating topic, quality, and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictors/topic of the study (Big Five vs astrological factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the predictors of the 40 behaviors (either Big Five or astrological factors)” — the thematic content or theoretical framework (e.g., mainstream personality factors vs astrology) of the research presented in the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The topic/predictor set is a manipulated variable in the study and strongly influences evaluators' judgments. The paper contrasts evaluations when abstracts present mainstream credible predictors (Big Five) versus controversial/less-credible predictors (astrology). Use of a controversial topic can trigger confirmation bias in readers; reviewers may rate identical methods/results differently depending on the topic's perceived plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological quality of the study (low, medium, high)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the methodological quality of the study (low, medium, high)” — abstracts were explicitly varied to represent different quality levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper operationalizes quality via concrete differences in abstract content: sample size (e.g., 187 vs 47 vs 27), number of independent raters (3 vs 1), analytic approach (regression analyses vs simple correlations), and how predictors were selected (judges/experts vs author-selected). Higher-quality abstracts include larger samples, multiple raters with reported interrater reliability, and more detailed/rigorous analyses. Lower-quality abstracts omit such details or report smaller samples and simpler analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results and subsequent conclusion (confirmation or disconfirmation of the hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the results and subsequent conclusion of the study (confirmation or disconfirmation of the hypotheses)” — whether reported findings support or refute the study hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dimension was manipulated between subjects. The study shows that evaluators' ratings of an abstract's quality/appropriateness depend on whether results align with their prior beliefs; abstracts whose conclusions conformed to readers' expectations were rated more favorably. When evaluating abstracts, consider how claims of confirmation vs disconfirmation are presented (strength of evidence, framing) and be aware of confirmation-bias tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality (dependent factor derived from 8 rating scales)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Factor-analyzed scores of participants’ ratings on 8 scales, resulting in 2 factors termed quality and appropriateness, served as dependent measures.” — one of the two outcome dimensions used to capture perceived study quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study, 'quality' is a composite latent factor from multiple rating items (not all listed on the page). When designing reviewer or reader rating forms, include multiple items tapping methodological rigor, clarity of methods, and statistical adequacy; these can be factor-analyzed into a general 'quality' score for use as an outcome or evaluation metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness (dependent factor derived from 8 rating scales)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second composite dependent measure, termed 'appropriateness', derived alongside 'quality' from the factor analysis of participants' ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriateness likely captures perceived fit between research question, methods, and conclusions (e.g., whether the study appropriately addresses the posed research question). Include items assessing relevance, fit of methods to aims, and appropriateness of interpretations to yield this factor in reviewer assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract completeness and structure (Purpose, Method, Results, Conclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendix abstracts consistently present sections labeled Purpose, Method, Results (excerpts), and interpretive Conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence and clarity of these structural components in an abstract are treated as indicators of quality. Well-structured abstracts succinctly state purpose, sample and procedure, key results (including numeric/statistical excerpts), and a clear conclusion. Missing or vague component descriptions are indicative of lower-quality abstracts in the manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical reporting (regression/correlation metrics, R, r, R1, R0, % variance explained, p-values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts include numeric/statistical details such as regression results (R1, R0), correlations (r), percentage increases in variance explained (%), and p-values (e.g., p < .05, p < .001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed statistical reporting (specifying analysis type and effect-size indicators) is modeled as a marker of higher methodological quality. Examples: reporting interrater reliability (.83), R1 and R0 with % increase, and exact p-values. Sparse or non-specific statistical reporting (e.g., only stating 'significant' without numbers) functions as a lower-quality signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and sampling description
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts explicitly report sample sizes (e.g., 'A total of 187 subjects', '47 undergraduate university students', '27 undergraduate university students') and basic demographic split (e.g., 97 female and 90 male).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger and better-described samples are used to operationalize higher methodological quality. When evaluating abstracts, scrutinize sample size, composition, and whether sampling procedures are described; small or poorly-described samples reduce confidence in generalizability and are treated as lower quality in the paper's manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rater procedures and interrater reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural details about raters (e.g., '3 astrologers rated them separately' and 'Because the interrater-reliability between the 3 astrologers was .83, the data of the three astrologers were collapsed together').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of multiple independent raters and reporting interrater reliability (and how ratings were aggregated) is a concrete marker of higher methodological rigor. Abstracts that include such information are treated as higher quality; absence suggests lower reliability of measures and lower quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of predictors by judges/experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural note used in some abstracts: 'An astrologer was asked to rate the expected association... then chose the highest rated facets as predictors' or 'Judges were asked to rate the expected association... and then the authors chose the five highest rated facets as predictors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether predictors were selected via expert/judge ratings versus by other methods is used to distinguish methodological approaches. Expert-driven predictor selection and transparent selection procedures are treated as more rigorous; opaque or convenience-driven predictor choice reduces perceived methodological quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic credibility / controversy as an influence on evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit criterion: topics vary in perceived scientific plausibility (e.g., astrology presented vs Big Five personality), and this credibility/controversy affects evaluators' judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper demonstrates that reviewers/readers may rate identical methods/results differently depending on the perceived credibility of the topic. When evaluating abstracts, be aware that topic plausibility can bias quality judgments; explicit safeguards (blinding to topic or preregistered evaluation criteria) can help reduce such bias.
